RT @MsftSecIntel: Microsoft Threat Intelligence is tracking an active supply chain attack in which a threat actor compromised the trusted OAuth App of the backup application ConnectWise Cloud Backup (AppId: 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae), formerly SkyKick Backup, to obtain access tokens across customer tenants. 

ConnectWise Cloud Backup is a multitenant vendor application; customers grant consent for the application to operate in their tenants. We assess that the threat actor likely abused permissions previously granted by customers to the application, including highly elevated permissions like Directory.ReadWrite.All.

On October 15, 2026, we observed broad successful service principal authentication originating from the IP address 144.172.64[.]128. Follow-on activity included Microsoft Graph API reconnaissance and attempts to add additional credentials on the related service principal in target tenants to maintain direct access as a backdoor. 

Microsoft Defender detects post-exploitation activity with the following alerts:
- Any alert related to "Suspicious sign-in"
- Graph API activity from a Microsoft threat intelligence IP address 
- Verified Threat Actor IP

Defenders should review service principal sign-ins from unrecognized IP addresses, app credential changes, and OAuth grant activity associated with this specific OAuth AppId. In addition, we recommend looking for Threat Intelligence alerts on matching of IP against the Graph API activity and service principal activities. 

We will continue to monitor this incident and will share updates as they become available. We encourage customers to check ConnectWise advisory for more information and additional guidance: https://t.co/zwFyMAzaEV.

Indicators of compromise (IOCs): 
- App name: ConnectWise Cloud Backup  
- AppId: 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae   
- Publisher name: SkyKick  
- Source IP: 144.172.64[.]128
- User agents: Python-urllib/3.12, python-requests/2.31, python-requests/2.34.2

items.content:
RT @m19o__: This is what happens when AI safety and alignment policies are designed without considering the people defending systems.

During the Hugging Face incident, commercial models blocked legitimate forensic analysis of real attack logs and payloads. They had to use a self-hosted GLM-5.2 to investigate the breach.

Now OpenCode is dealing with another security incident involving exposed AI provider keys, raising further questions about how dependent defenders are on the providers they rely on.

We’re past the point of using fearmongering about AI falling into the wrong hands to justify keeping advanced capabilities behind closed doors.

I’m not arguing against safeguards. I’m arguing that safeguards shouldn’t prevent legitimate security work.

If you don’t want to open-source your models, fine. At least establish a practical process that gives defenders access to the capabilities they need for research, testing, and incident response.

And by defenders, I mean everyone working in cybersecurity, not just a handful of organizations selected by AI labs.

This chain is interesting. 1-click Remote Code Execution via Twitch Embed.

Basically you start with a webpage that triggers discord to render a crafted Twitch rich embed. by exploiting a gap in Twitch's HLS manifest parsing, you can redirect the media flow to an attacker controlled playlist and execute a custom OMID ad-verification script inside a discord popout context. From there the chain moves into V8, where a regexp use afterfree vulnerability is leveraged to turn a memory corruption bug into more reliable read & write capabilities.

items.content:
A developer checked the source code and confirmed that no API token had been hardcoded.

The configuration file was also protected, so everyone assumed the secret was safe.

But the application received the token through an environment variable. Once the service started, that variable became part of the running process and could be inspected through Linux’s /proc filesystem.

In the image, PID 3412 belongs to the Inventory API running as www-data. Reading /proc/3412/environ reveals the application environment, database host, database username and a redacted lab token.

The /proc file is not readable by every ordinary user. Access depends on process ownership, root privileges and security controls such as hidepid and ptrace restrictions. Still, an administrator—or an attacker who gains sufficient privileges—may be able to recover secrets from a live process.

Environment variables are better than hardcoding credentials, but they are not automatically secret storage. Sensitive values should be protected with proper service permissions, short-lived credentials, restricted /proc access and a dedicated secrets-management system.

The secret may be absent from the source code and still be sitting inside the process.

The potential impact of the ConnectWise supply chain attack is massive.

One compromised OAuth application with elevated permissions could give attackers access to emails, files, and directory data across hundreds of Microsoft 365 tenants.

Even worse, attackers could establish persistent access by adding credentials to other applications, surviving the revocation of the original compromised credentials.

And with MSPs involved, the potential blast radius could extend even further to downstream customers.

We don't know the full extent of the compromise yet, but this could affect far more organizations than those directly using ConnectWise Cloud Backup.

The industry used to have the luxury of testing or sitting on a fix for months. Not anymore. When everyone's using the same tools and the same intelligence to find vulnerabilities, you're not the only one finding that bug.

items.content:
RT @cr3ghost: This @BeyondTrust incident is worth reading, especially if you work in detection engineering or threat hunting.

@Mandiant says ARMORY CASTLE exploited CVE-2026-102764 in BeyondTrust Remote Support as a zero-day.

Post-exploitation got ugly:

- SAWFLY PHP webshell
- Service account -> root
- Attempted credential vault extraction
- Persistent passwordless root access
- Systematic log deletion
- BARECLAW WebSocket/SOCKS5 tunneler
- Admin session abuse
- Pivoting into downstream systems

But the part defenders should read twice:

BeyondTrust says its sensors fired high-severity alerts in real time when the actor escalated privileges.

A third-party automated triage system closed them as false positives.

Their separate threat-intelligence-driven hunting pipeline later surfaced the activity.

That is such an important detection engineering lesson.

Having telemetry and alerts is only part of the job. You still need strong detection engineering, active threat hunting, validation, R&D and people who understand what the adversary is actually doing.

The sensors saw it. The surrounding detection process failed to escalate it.

Excellent research and transparency from the @Mandiant and @BeyondTrust teams.

Mandiant technical analysis:

https://t.co/VKtJNieITB

BeyondTrust incident timeline + BT26-05:
https://t.co/idoCM0s1wX

Patch BT26-05 and read both write-ups.

items.content:
Andrii and the SOC Prime team have just launched LogTotal and I find the concept quite interesting

You can upload a collection of security logs, run detection rules against the events, correlate the matches into potential attack chains, and use AI to help interpret the results.
What I particularly like is the architecture. Instead of throwing millions of log events at an LLM, it starts with detection rules and correlation, using AI later in the process to help investigate and explain the findings.

Another interesting detail is the approach to privacy. Sensitive identifiers can be pseudonymized locally before uploading the logs. The sanitizer is even available as open source, with a CLI that can run completely offline. So if you don't want to rely on JavaScript delivered by a website, you can inspect the code and sanitize your logs in your own environment before uploading.

Sanitizer: https://t.co/VpMx44CZC7

I think that's a sensible direction for AI-assisted security investigations. It also makes retrospective log analysis accessible without having to set up an entire SIEM infrastructure.

I haven't tested it myself yet, and I'd be more interested in the quality of the detections and correlations than the advertised rule count or processing speed.

But the approach makes sense to me. Definitely worth a closer look.
